svg.text: ESD and EMI — the housing does the work, the PCB stays out of the way
A sealed metal camera with one cable has a small, well-defined threat surface. Almost every joule of an ESD event should end up in the chassis without ever meeting a PCB net.
The protection components are cheap; the topology decisions are not reversible once the housing is machined. Settle the grounding architecture before the mechanical drawing is released.
A · WHERE ESD GETS IN
IEC 61000-4-2, ±8 kV contact / ±15 kV air
aluminium housing — chassis node
RJ45
M8 I/O
tripod / bracket
Lens face, air discharge.
Metal barrel and mount, conductive gasket to the housing,
sensor-board guard ring bonded to the mount.
RJ45 shell, contact.
Shielded jack, 360° shell-to-chassis bond at the connector —
never a pigtail. Handled on the TIDA board.
Field I/O, contact.
TVS3300 per line on the field side, already fitted. Isolation
barrier stops the rest.
Bracket and screw heads.
Chassis to chassis. Goes nowhere near logic ground if the
topology in B is respected.
Sensor FPC, during service.
Not a field threat in a sealed camera. Controlled by ANSI/ESD
S20.20 handling, plus a 0.5 pF array on the low-speed lines.
B · GROUNDING TOPOLOGY
two nodes, one bond — decide this before the housing drawing is released
CHASSIS — housing, lens mount, RJ45 shell, standoffs
LOGIC GND — all three boards, one continuous node
DC bond
one only
at the cable end
1 nF / 2 kV × 3
remaining mounting holes
HF return, no DC loop
Alternative, fitted as DNF: drop the DC bond, make all four
capacitive, and let the TIDA board's 1 MΩ ∥ 1 nF network be
the only chassis reference. Choose that in a chamber, not here.
Never fit both bonds and then wonder.
A hard DC bond on the carrier shorts out the TIDA
board's 1 MΩ ∥ 1 nF network. That may well be what you
want — but it should be a decision, not a side effect.
The 1 nF capacitors are 2 kV parts, X7R, 0603.
They will see the full ESD transient. A 50 V 0402 in
this position fails short, and a shorted HF bond is a DC
bond you did not design.
Chassis copper is not logic copper.
The chassis node exists only as annular rings around the
mounting holes and the connector shells. It never
becomes a plane and never carries a return current.
Bond the lens mount to the housing, not to the sensor board.
An ESD hit on the front face must reach the housing
without transiting a 0.2 mm-thick PCB ground pour.
C · EMI — SOURCE, PATH, ANTENNA
fix whichever link is cheapest; it is almost never the source
SOURCE
4 MHz PoL switch nodes, ~1 V/ns
DDR3L 400 MHz CK, knee ≈ 2.5 GHz
MIPI 750 Mb/s, T_r ≈ 150 ps, knee ≈ 3.3 GHz
RGMII 125 MHz DDR, knee ≈ 1 GHz
Forced PWM, not PFM — a fixed 4 MHz comb
filters; PFM subharmonics do not.
Hot loop under 2 mm². DRIVE=4 on RGMII if
timing closes — the slew is free margin.
PATH
Common-mode current onto the CAT6 cable
The 60 mm sensor FPC, radiating inside the can
Aperture leakage at the lens and housing seams
Via fence at 2.5 mm = λ/20 at 3 GHz in Dk 3.9.
1.25 mm near the D-PHY escape and connectors.
π filter on every rail entering the flex; ground
flood both flex layers. No plane split, anywhere.
ANTENNA
The cable. Always the cable.
λ/4 at 30 MHz is 2.5 m — it is resonant in band
somewhere across 30 MHz to 1 GHz, whatever you do.
360° shell bond at the RJ45. Bob Smith
termination and the chassis capacitor are already
on the TIDA board — do not defeat them with a
second ground path through the carrier.
The lens aperture is not a leak.
A Ø12 mm metal barrel is a circular waveguide with a
TE₁₁ cutoff of f_c = 1.841c / 2πa ≈ 14.6 GHz. Below
cutoff it attenuates roughly 32 dB per barrel-length /
diameter. Everything in this design is far below 14.6 GHz,
so the hole radiates nothing — provided the barrel is
metal and bonded. A plastic mount throws that away.
THE MIPI TRADE-OFF, DECIDED
PROTECTION BILL OF MATERIALS
PRE-COMPLIANCE PLAN
No ESD diodes on the MIPI pairs. DNF footprints only.
At 750 Mb/s the knee is 3.3 GHz. A 0.3 pF shunt is 161 Ω
there — on a 50 Ω line that is a real discontinuity, and
the pair already carries connector and land capacitance.
The flex never leaves the housing.
It is exposed exactly once, on the bench, by someone
wearing a wrist strap. That is a process control, not a
component.
Fit the array if the flex ever becomes field-serviceable.
Then the answer inverts: ≤ 0.3 pF per line, placed between
the connector and the FPGA so the stub is on the protected
side.
TPD4E05U06 — carrier, at the FPC.
0.5 pF, 4 channels: I²C, RESET_BAR, TRIGGER, FLASH.
TVS3300 ×4 — TIDA board, field side.
Already fitted. Flat-clamp, so the clamp voltage does not
run away with current.
1 nF / 2 kV X7R 0603 ×3 — carrier.
Chassis HF bonds at three mounting holes.
Ferrite bead + 1 µF ×4 — carrier.
π filter per rail at the sensor flex. 600 Ω at 100 MHz,
rated for the DC load current.
Worst-case pattern first.
DDR3L memtest, MIPI at the maximum lane rate, and RGMII at
line rate, all at once. A camera streaming 17 fps is not a
test.
Near-field probe before the chamber.
An hour with a 5 mm loop finds more than a day of chamber
time, and it is the only way to tell which of the three
links in C is actually costing you.
Define the immunity criterion before you book the slot.
'No dropped frames, no I²C lockup, no link renegotiation'
is testable. 'Works fine' is not.
